title: Meta would 'consider' pulling services from Canada if lawful access bill passes as is
summary: Representatives from Meta say the social media company would have to "consider" pulling encryption services from Canada if the government's proposed lawful access bill passes without further changes.

image.caption: Meta services include Facebook, Instagram and the encrypted messaging app WhatsApp. (Richard Drew/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Politics·Updated
Representatives from Meta say the social media company would have to "consider" pulling encryption services from Canada if the government's proposed lawful access bill passes without further changes.
Company says government amendments don't protect encrypted data
Bill C-22 would force tech companies to adapt their systems so they all have the ability to hand over information to investigators with a warrant.

The legislation is currently being studied in the Senate, where Meta representatives said the bill leaves encrypted information — meant only to be viewed by users sharing the information — vulnerable to malicious actors.

"Ultimately, the Canadian government would be enforcing and imposing a law that it is not technically feasible to comply with and still offer secure, end-to-end encrypted services to Canadians," Robyn Greene, Meta's director of privacy and public policy, told senators on the national security committee on Monday evening.
Meta services include Facebook, Instagram and the encrypted messaging app WhatsApp.

When asked if the legislation would mean the company would pull some of its services from Canada, Meta's head of public policy for Canada Rachel Curran said the company would have to "review all of our options."
But she said it is something the company would have to "consider."
Minister of Public Safety Gary Anandasangaree proposed amendments to the lawful access legislation, but critics say they don't go far enough. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

Bill C-22 also grants the minister the authority to issue confidential ministerial orders to electronic service providers (ESPs) operating in Canada, requiring them to build surveillance and monitoring capabilities into their systems. Orders would first be reviewed by the intelligence commissioner — an independent quasi-judicial official.
Before the bill was sent to the Senate in June, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree brought in amendments that put limits on when companies would be required to decrypt information.

Another change reduces the length of time that tech companies would have to retain metadata to six months from up to a year, after cybersecurity experts warned that data would be an attractive target for hackers.

blocks.text: Curran told the Senate committee that the government's amendments don't go far enough to protect encrypted data.
"They have protected just the core and not the outside layers that are an integral part of the encryption process," she said.
Encrypted messaging service Signal has also consistently said it would withdraw from Canada if the bill passes.
"If we are forced to choose between betraying our users and leaving Canada, we will not compromise the security of Canadians," Signal vice-president Udbhav Tiwari told the Senate committee.
Tiwari called on the government to make further changes to the bill, including explicit assurances to protect encrypted data.
Tech giant Apple also said earlier this month that the amendments aren't enough.

"While we appreciate attempts to improve C-22, the bill could still undermine Apple's ability to offer the powerful privacy and security features our users expect from us, including encryption, even as AI and other evolving technologies provide hackers with new tools to exploit cybersecurity weaknesses," the company said in a statement.
Privacy watchdog calls for changes

The government has argued that the bill is needed to ensure law enforcement has the legal tools to prevent, investigate and respond to modern crime and protect Canadians. Still, the proposed legislation has faced consistent pushback and this is the second lawful access bill the government has introduced this session.
Earlier this month, Privacy Commissioner Philippe Dufresne urged the Senate committee to further amend the legislation to better protect the privacy of Canadians.

The bill would lower the legal threshold for law enforcement and intelligence bodies to access basic subscriber information — like names, addresses, telephone numbers, email addresses and account numbers — from "reasonable grounds to believe" down to "reasonable grounds to suspect" that an offence has been or will be committed.
Dufresne said the definition of subscriber information and who can be asked to hand it over remain overly broad relative to the lowered threshold required to access it.
